front: Worked: VD on a 1φ 120 V, 16 A load, 150 ft one-way, 12 AWG Cu (6530 cmil)
Worked: minimum CM to hold 3 % on 1φ 240 V, 30 A, 200 ft one-way, copper
Worked: 3φ VD — 480 V, 40 A, 300 ft one-way, 8 AWG Cu (16,510 cmil)
Worked: line current of a 3φ 480 V, 75 kVA load
back:
I = kVA × 1000 ÷ (1.732 × V)
= 75,000 ÷ (1.732 × 480)
= 75,000 ÷ 831.4 ≈ 90.2 A
Same formula sizes transformer secondaries: 75 kVA at 208 V → 208 A

front: Worked: current of a 1φ 240 V, 10 kW resistive heater; then with PF 0.8
back:
Resistive (PF 1): I = P ÷ V = 10,000 ÷ 240 = 41.7 A
With PF 0.8: I = P ÷ (V × PF) = 10,000 ÷ 192 = 52.1 A
Lower power factor → more amps for the same watts

front: Worked: 1φ transformer, 480 V primary → 120 V secondary, 60 A secondary load
back:
Ratio = 480 ÷ 120 = 4:1
Primary current = 60 ÷ 4 = 15 A
Check with kVA: 120 × 60 = 7.2 kVA; 7200 ÷ 480 = 15 A ✔
Voltage steps down, current steps up by the same ratio

front: Worked: input current of a 10 HP, 1φ 240 V motor at 85 % efficiency, PF 0.9 (theory, not the NEC table)
back:
Output W = 10 × 746 = 7460 W
Input W = 7460 ÷ 0.85 = 8776 W
I = W ÷ (V × PF) = 8776 ÷ (240 × 0.9) = 40.6 A
For 3φ divide by 1.732 × V × PF
NEC sizing still uses Table 430.248/430.250 FLC, not this math

front: Worked: a load draws 50 kVA with 40 kW — find PF, kVAR and the angle
back:
PF = kW ÷ kVA = 40 ÷ 50 = 0.80
kVAR = √(kVA² − kW²) = √(2500 − 1600) = 30 kVAR
θ = arccos 0.80 ≈ 36.9°
Adding capacitors cuts the kVAR, raises PF toward 1.0

front: Worked: series R = 30 Ω, XL = 40 Ω on 120 V — Z, I, PF
back:
Z = √(R² + XL²) = √(900 + 1600) = 50 Ω
I = V ÷ Z = 120 ÷ 50 = 2.4 A
PF = R ÷ Z = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60 lagging
If XC were present: X = XL − XC before squaring

front: Worked: XL of a 0.1 H coil and XC of a 50 µF capacitor at 60 Hz
Worked: total resistance of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel
back:
1 ÷ Rt = 1/10 + 1/20 + 1/30 = 0.1 + 0.05 + 0.0333 = 0.1833
Rt = 1 ÷ 0.1833 ≈ 5.45 Ω
Always less than the smallest branch (10 Ω)
Two resistors shortcut: R1 × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2)

front: Worked: 120 V across 10 Ω + 20 Ω + 30 Ω in series — current and each drop
back:
Rt = 60 Ω; I = 120 ÷ 60 = 2 A everywhere
Drops: 20 V, 40 V, 60 V (sum = 120 V, Kirchhoff)
Power: 40 W, 80 W, 120 W — the biggest resistor dissipates the most in series

front: Worked: resistance of 500 ft of 10 AWG Cu (10,380 cmil) using K = 12.9
back:
R = K × L ÷ CM = 12.9 × 500 ÷ 10,380 ≈ 0.62 Ω
Ch. 9 Table 8 cross-check: 10 AWG uncoated Cu ≈ 1.21 Ω per 1000 ft → 0.61 Ω for 500 ft ✔
Double the length = double the R; double the CM = half the R

front: Worked: 208Y/120 V system, each phase load 20 A — line current and total kVA
back:
Wye: line current = phase current = 20 A; line voltage = 120 × 1.732 = 208 V
kVA = 1.732 × 208 × 20 ÷ 1000 = 7.2 kVA
(or 3 × 120 × 20 = 7200 VA — same answer)
Delta flips it: line current = 1.732 × phase current, line V = phase V

front: Worked: cost to run a 1500 W heater 8 h/day for 30 days at $0.15/kWh
back:
kWh = 1.5 kW × 8 h × 30 = 360 kWh
Cost = 360 × $0.15 = $54.00
Watts ÷ 1000 → kW; × hours → kWh; × rate → dollars

front: Worked: 120/240 V 3-wire with 18 A on L1 and 11 A on L2 — neutral current? And on a 208Y/120 V 3-phase 4-wire with 18 A / 11 A / 0 A?
back:
1φ 3-wire: neutral = difference = 18 − 11 = 7 A
3φ 4-wire (two phases loaded): In = √(a² + b² − ab) = √(324 + 121 − 198) = √247 ≈ 15.7 A
Three equal phase loads → neutral ≈ 0 (balanced)

front: Worked: a 120 V RMS sine wave — peak and peak-to-peak; a 170 V peak — RMS
back:
Peak = RMS × 1.414 = 169.7 V; peak-to-peak ≈ 339 V
RMS = peak × 0.707 = 170 × 0.707 ≈ 120 V
Meters read RMS; insulation sees peak

front: Worked: a 1200 W, 120 V appliance — current, resistance, and power if run at 240 V (same R)
back:
I = 1200 ÷ 120 = 10 A
R = V ÷ I = 120 ÷ 10 = 12 Ω
At 240 V: P = V² ÷ R = 57,600 ÷ 12 = 4800 W — doubling voltage quadruples power (and burns it up)
